payload.because: Posting ourselves buys an undocumented wire format, an own-child verification rule that macOS can only satisfy while the poster is still running, inbound controls that HOLD non-child posts for user approval in any bypassPermissions session, and a delivered message billed to the user like a typed prompt. Worse, the exemption and the value are in tension: the socket's unique benefit is waking an IDLE session, and an idle session runs no hooks, so nothing of ours is alive to be its child. Channels are the doc-sanctioned path for external push but are closed to us — research preview, Anthropic auth, Bun, a restart with --channels, and only Anthropic-allowlisted plugins may register. Addressing has none of these failure modes: the agent doing the sending is already inside the host that owns the channel, so it sends under its own permissions, on its own turn, with its own tool. The mapping was the one open question and it is now verified live (2026-08-08, claude 2.1.226): the registry's sessionId is byte-identical to the session id sofar already stores from the hook JSON, and `name` is the address. Degradation is structural rather than disciplined — no registry, no address, and every surface renders exactly what it rendered before, which is asserted byte-for-byte in the tests. felt-cost D3 holds untouched: we hand over a string and call nothing.
payload.chose: sofar resolves the ADDRESS, Claude's own SendMessage delivers: read the host's undocumented ~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json registry to map a Claude Code session id to the name SendMessage addresses, and annotate the two collision surfaces that already name that id (2.1's UserPromptSubmit line, 1.2's parallel_writebacks).
payload.over: sofar posting directly into CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_SOCKET (the first sketch), and building on Claude Code channels — the surface the messaging docs actually route external-event push to
payload.rule: Peer resolution is an optional last inch: sofar must never bind an inbox socket or send a message itself, and no surface may become correct only when a peer resolves — the record-side line has to stand alone.

payload.text:
MEASURED 2026-08-08: cost of cross-initiative file-conflict detection, against the speed T2 100ms end-to-end shim budget. Measured on this repo (30 initiatives, 6672 events, 4.7MB — almost certainly the largest sofar record that exists, so a good worst case).

Baseline: the real installed `sofar event user-prompt-submit` shim on this repo runs 63-67ms end-to-end (8 runs). Headroom ~35ms.

Fold costs, in-process, median of 15:
- fold 1 biggest initiative (token-optimization, 663 events) + conflicts: 1.8ms
- fold 1 current branch (peer-messaging, tiny): 0.2ms
- fold ALL 30 + union conflicts: 15.8ms
- stat 30 + fold ONLY logs written in the last 12h (3 of 30): 1.7ms

Conclusion: naive all-initiative folding costs +15.8ms — it PASSES today (~79-83ms) but is O(total history), so it degrades forever and a repo with 100+ initiatives blows the budget. The mtime gate collapses it to +1.7ms, a 9x reduction, and changes the scaling: cost then tracks CONCURRENT ACTIVITY (bounded by open terminals), not accumulated history.

The gate is principled, not a fudge: the hazard is CONCURRENT EDITING, and a session that is concurrently editing is appending events continuously (PostToolUse fires on every tool call). A log not written in 12h cannot hold a session that is editing right now.

Known degradation: mtime is not append-only — `git checkout` rewrites every events.jsonl and would make all 30 look recent, falling back to the 15.8ms all-fold path. Bounded, rare, still inside budget.

Verdict: buildable and cheap WITH the gate; do not build it without one.

Gate is principled: concurrent editing appends events continuously, so a cold log cannot hold a live editor. Numbers recorded as a note. Nothing built — awaiting a ruling.
